description:
Barony Castle stands in the Eddleston valley near Peebles in the Scottish Borders, a landscape that once bristled with small fortified towers built specifically to withstand the centuries of raiding and reiving that defined life along the medieval Anglo-Scottish frontier. The oldest structure on the site was one such peel tower, raised in the early 15th century as one of roughly a dozen similar defensive towers scattered along this single valley — a striking concentration that speaks to just how contested and insecure this stretch of country was for the ordinary landholding families who lived here.

The estate's documented ownership begins in 1506, when King James IV granted the lands of Haltoun to John Murray of Fallahill, who was made Laird of Blackbarony. The family's fortunes were tied closely to the crown they served: Murray's son, Sir John, died fighting alongside King James IV at the catastrophic Battle of Flodden in 1513, one of the darkest single days in Scottish military history, in which the king and much of the Scottish nobility perished.

The peel tower was substantially built over in 1536, when a proper Scots Baronial building — then known by the name 'Darnhall' — was raised on the same foundations, transforming the old defensive structure into a more comfortable and status-appropriate residence for the Murray family. The house continued to evolve over the following centuries: between 1700 and 1715, a grand French and Jacobean-influenced façade was added, a renovation contemporaries described as more elegant than any other house in the county, reflecting the family's continued prosperity and taste well into the early 18th century.

What sets Barony Castle apart most distinctively from every other property in this entire pilot collection, however, has nothing to do with its medieval or Georgian architecture. The estate's grounds hold the Great Polish Map of Scotland — an extraordinary outdoor concrete relief model, measuring 50 by 40 metres, depicting the topography of Scotland in three dimensions at a scale visitors can walk across. It was built between 1974 and 1979 by Jan Tomasik, a Polish war veteran who had settled in Scotland after the Second World War, and it is widely considered the largest relief model of an entire country to be found anywhere in the world — a genuinely singular monument with no real equivalent among Scotland's castle-hotel grounds.

The map holds Category B listed status, and after falling into disrepair it was fully restored and reopened to the public on 12 April 2018. What makes this restoration especially significant for visitors is not simply that the map is open to the public as a matter of policy, the way an afternoon tea or a bistro might be at other properties in this collection — it is that the hotel is contractually obligated to guarantee free public access to the map, under the binding terms of the original restoration funding, which included support from the Heritage Lottery Fund. This is a categorically stronger form of public access than anywhere else documented in this pilot: not a hospitable business choice that could theoretically change, but a legal condition attached to the grant money that restored the map in the first place, meaning any visitor can walk the grounds and examine this remarkable structure regardless of whether they are staying at the hotel, dining there, or have any other business on the property at all.

faqs.question: Do I need to be a hotel guest to see the Great Polish Map of Scotland?
faqs.answer: No — and this is the strongest form of guaranteed public access anywhere in this collection of castle-hotels. Under the binding terms of the restoration grants that funded the map's 2018 reopening, including Heritage Lottery Fund support, the hotel is contractually required to provide free public access to the map regardless of whether a visitor is staying overnight, dining, or has any other business at the property.

faqs.question: What is the Great Polish Map of Scotland?
faqs.answer: It is an outdoor concrete relief model of Scotland's topography, measuring 50 by 40 metres, built between 1974 and 1979 by Jan Tomasik, a Polish war veteran who settled in the area after the Second World War. It is widely considered the largest relief model of an entire country anywhere in the world, and holds Category B listed status following its full restoration and reopening on 12 April 2018.

faqs.question: What is the origin of the castle building itself?
